## The four o’clock toast

I finished my last night shift on Sunday morning. Saturday, 21:00 to 07:30, in majors. Fourteen years of nights, and then I went home.

From Monday, I’m on the days-only rota. My knees and my sleep have been making the case for a while. My GP recently added that my blood pressure was not a joke any more, which was inconvenient because jokes were most of my treatment plan.

It is a sensible change. I wanted it. I’m relieved.

I am also, to my considerable irritation, sad.

I haven’t written here since spring, and I’ve made several attempts at this post already. One sounded like an obituary for someone who is still alive and will be back at work on Monday. Another became a complaint about the NHS. I have written enough of those, and that isn’t what I want to say this time.

I’m not leaving emergency medicine. I’m not even leaving the department. I am going to see the same people, use the same computers and have the same arguments with the same computers, only at hours when it is reasonable to have eaten breakfast.

Still, something has finished. I don’t quite know what to do with that.

***

My first night shift was as an SHO in 2012. I can’t remember much about the shift itself now. I wish I could offer a useful first impression, but what remains of that time is less orderly than that.

I remember the car park at the Infirmary during my first winter of nights. I was crying because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose.

I had. That was checked. There was no missed dose.

But I can still remember the frost on the windscreen.

Fourteen years later, that is the detail that has stayed clear. Not the reassurance afterwards, or what I did when I got home. Just sitting there, frightened by the possibility that I had forgotten something important, looking at the frost.

I got better at the work. I got better at knowing when to ask, when to check again, when the unease meant something and when it meant I needed sleep. I never became someone who could always leave a shift behind on the way out of the building.

Some mornings it came home with me. I don’t want to pretend that was noble. It was tiring, and sometimes it made me poor company.

***

People tend to think nights in emergency medicine are about adrenaline. Occasionally they are. Mostly, though, they are about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

Listening properly when someone is taking a long time to explain. Answering a question without letting your exhaustion sound like annoyance. Remembering that the person in front of you hasn’t been there for the previous eight hours and isn’t responsible for them.

I didn’t always manage it. There were shifts when I was brisker than I needed to be, and mornings when that was the thing I regretted.

But I worked with people who did manage it, over and over, and who helped me manage it too. Sometimes by being kind to me. Sometimes by giving me a look.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has done this for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs. I would like to attribute that entirely to my knees, but I suspect she would have beaten me in 2012 as well.

It is difficult to explain what it means to work with someone for whom the middle of the night is familiar territory. Not easy territory. Just somewhere they know how to be. There is a particular reassurance in seeing that person when you come in.

I will miss that.

***

I’ve always thought nights are when the department is most itself. There are fewer managers about, which helps, but it’s more than that. People tend to say what they mean. There is less energy available for pretending, and often more kindness than you would expect from a group of people who ought to be asleep.

Not every night. I’m not going to become sentimental enough to claim that tiredness brings out the best in everyone. It doesn’t. Sometimes it brings out the worst, or simply leaves you with very little to offer.

But I’ve known a lot of quiet kindness at night.

A patient once held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. I won’t say more about him here. It was a brief moment, and probably meant something different to each of us. I’ve kept it all the same.

Then there is the toast.

At about four in the morning, someone makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. I don’t know how this arrangement works, and after fourteen years I have made no serious attempt to investigate.

You become aware of the smell. At some point there is toast.

There are plenty of things I could say about teamwork, but I’m not sure any would improve on that.

***

Nights gave me friendships I would have struggled to make anywhere else. They gave me confidence, eventually, and a fairer understanding of my limits. They let me see colleagues being funny, patient and generous when none of those things was easy.

They also took things.

Sleep, obviously. Though “sleep” seems too small a word for the amount of life that gets organised around trying to obtain it. The day before a night. The day after. Being technically free but not really available. Saying yes to something and then spending it wishing you were horizontal.

I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies, even over video, because of nights. My sister in Bangalore never once complained.

I don’t know why that makes it harder to write about, but it does. She understood. I was grateful that she understood. I still wish she hadn’t needed to.

There is a temptation, looking back, to make a tidy account of it: these were the sacrifices, these were the rewards, and therefore it was worth it. I can’t do that. I loved parts of this life, and I missed things I cannot go back and attend now.

My body has also become rather less willing to negotiate. At forty-two, I had hoped to get a bit further on stubbornness. Apparently blood pressure does not recognise length of service.

So I am stopping nights. Before being forced to stop, and with considerable relief.

The relief is the part that makes me feel like a traitor.

I know how unreasonable that is. If a colleague told me their sleep was poor, their knees hurt and their GP was worried about their blood pressure, I would not suggest they demonstrate loyalty by continuing indefinitely. I would tell them to take the days-only rota.

I’m trying to extend myself the same courtesy. It is taking longer than expected.

***

I drove home down the London Road on Sunday morning with the sun coming up and the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up.

The forecast was going about its business. I was tired. It was a journey I had made many times.

And then I realised I would not see that light from this side again.

Of course I will be awake at sunrise again. I may even be driving down the same road. But I won’t be coming out of a night shift, with the department still running through my head and everyone else’s morning beginning around me.

I hadn’t known I would miss that light until I was in it for the last time.

I carried on home. There wasn’t anything else to do.

I hope days will give me back some ordinary things: better sleep, a body that complains less, a little more ability to be present when I’m not at work. I’m looking forward to finding out. I expect I’ll miss nights unevenly, and that some weeks I won’t miss them at all.

The night team will carry on without me, as it should. Folasade will still be beating people up the stairs.

And at about four, someone will put the toast on.
